reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Beau lines are transverse grooves running across the nail plate parallel to the lunula, marking a temporary slowing of matrix activity
When several nails are affected at the same level the cause is usually systemic, such as a severe febrile illness, chemotherapy, or major metabolic upset
A single affected nail more often reflects local trauma to that particular matrix
The distance of the groove from the proximal nail fold allows the timing of the insult to be estimated from the known rate of nail growth
Complete arrest of the matrix produces total-thickness separation and shedding, which is termed onychomadesis and lies at the severe end of the same spectrum
They are retrospective markers of a past event rather than an active disease requiring treatment of the nail itself
Reassurance is appropriate once a self-limited precipitant is identified, as the groove grows out with the nail
reference.pathophysiology: Beau lines result from a transient interruption of proximal nail matrix function that temporarily reduces the production of nail plate. During the period of impaired activity a thinner segment of plate is laid down, which appears as a transverse depression once that portion emerges from beneath the proximal nail fold and grows distally. Any insult severe enough to divert resources away from the matrix, whether a systemic illness, cytotoxic therapy, nutritional or metabolic disturbance, or direct local trauma, can produce the groove, and the depth of the furrow reflects the severity and duration of the interruption.
additionalDifferentials: Onychomadesis (complete matrix arrest with plate shedding)
Habit-tic deformity producing washboard transverse ridging
Longitudinal ridging of ageing (distinguished by orientation)
Nail changes of eczema or psoriasis affecting the proximal fold
Transverse leukonychia (Mees' lines) from toxic exposure
additionalInvestigations: History to identify a preceding febrile illness, chemotherapy, or metabolic event
Examination of all nails to determine whether one or many are affected
Estimation of the timing of the insult from the groove position and nail growth rate
Screening for systemic illness or nutritional deficiency if the cause is unclear
Onychoscopy to distinguish true matrix grooves from surface ridging
Review of recent medications, particularly cytotoxic agents
redFlags: Multiple nails affected together, pointing to a significant systemic illness that warrants explanation
Recurrent regular Beau lines suggesting cyclical systemic disease or repeated chemotherapy cycles
Progression to complete plate shedding (onychomadesis) indicating severe matrix arrest
Beau lines with other signs of serious underlying disease requiring further workup
reference.prognosis: Beau lines are self-limiting and grow out completely over several months as the nail advances, provided the precipitating event does not recur, and they require no specific treatment of the nail.
pitfalls: Treating the nail groove itself instead of investigating and addressing the systemic trigger
Failing to distinguish widespread systemic Beau lines from a single traumatic nail
Confusing surface habit-tic ridging with true matrix-derived Beau lines
Missing recurrent lines that signal cyclical illness or repeated drug exposure
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Reassure that the grooves are a retrospective marker of a past insult that grows out over months and need no treatment of the nail itself
Identify and address the precipitating systemic cause, such as a severe febrile illness, chemotherapy or metabolic disturbance, to prevent recurrence
For a single affected nail, protect the digit from further local trauma to the matrix
Correct any underlying nutritional deficiency and review recent cytotoxic or other implicated medications
Monitor for onychomadesis (complete nail-plate shedding), which lies at the severe end of the same spectrum
Refer for dermatological review only if the cause remains unexplained or multiple nails are progressively affected
